summary: Describes how Segment Routing over MPLS works in networks that also run LDP, including where some nodes support Segment Routing and others do not. It lets operators migrate gradually while paths keep working across both kinds of nodes.

eli5.summary: When a school switches to a new bus system, old and new buses must still share routes. This explains how to mix the two so nobody is stranded.

subtitle: How Segment Routing and LDP share one MPLS network, so operators can adopt SR a piece at a time.

tldr.problem: Networks that already run LDP cannot switch every router to Segment Routing at once, so SR-capable and non-SR-capable routers have to work together.
tldr.mechanism: SR and LDP use separate label ranges so they can coexist, SR nodes stitch LDP labels to SR labels at the border, and a Segment Routing Mapping Server advertises SIDs on behalf of routers that lack SR.
tldr.outcome: Operators can run SR next to LDP, use SR only for things like fast reroute protection of LDP traffic, and migrate gradually. RFC 8661 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8661 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2019. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR, RFC 8402) can run on the MPLS data plane without any modification, as described in RFC 8660. Its control plane can coexist with label distribution protocols such as LDP (RFC 5036).

This document describes how SR interworks with LDP when SR-capable and non-SR-capable routers sit in the same routing domain. Section 2 covers coexistence, Section 3 interworking, Section 4 use cases for partial SR deployment, and Appendix A a migration method.

Typically an implementation lets the operator choose by configuration which of the described modes of coexistence to use.
sections.eli5: Some routers speak the new language and some only the old one. This document is the phrasebook that lets them cooperate.

sections.title: Ships-in-the-Night Coexistence
sections.content:
An MPLS Control-Plane Client (MCC) is any protocol that installs forwarding entries in the MPLS data plane. SR, LDP, RSVP-TE and BGP are examples. Each MCC must make sure the incoming labels it installs have been uniquely allocated to itself.

SR gets this through the Segment Routing Global Block (SRGB), a range of labels reserved for it. For prefix segments the operator ensures each global label is unique within the SRGB, and adjacency segments are local labels allocated by the label manager like any other. This lets SR coexist with any other MCC.

The RFC's example runs an ODD VPN service over LDP and an EVEN VPN service over SR across the same routers A, B and C. Router A holds both an LDP entry (incoming label 1037, outgoing 2048) and an SR entry (incoming 203, outgoing 203) for the same prefix. They coexist because their incoming labels are unique. The same holds for entries that pop the label and forward as IP (MPLS2IP).
sections.eli5: LDP and SR each get their own set of numbered lockers, so they never fight over the same locker even in the same building.

sections.title: Interworking Between LDP and SR
sections.content:
Here SR runs in one part of the network and LDP in another, and the goal is one continuous MPLS tunnel across both.

LDP to SR needs no extra signaling or state. An SR node with LDP neighbors MUST create LDP bindings for each Prefix-SID learned in the SR domain, treating SR-learned labels as if an LDP neighbor had sent them, and stitch the incoming LDP label to the outgoing SR label. This applies in both LDP-independent and ordered label distribution modes. In the RFC's example, router P6 has no LDP binding from its next hop for FEC PE1, so it swaps its LDP label for node segment 101.

SR to LDP is harder because the LDP-only routers do not advertise SIDs. It needs a Segment Routing Mapping Server (SRMS), an IGP node that advertises mappings between SIDs and prefixes of other nodes. An SR node with LDP-only neighbors MUST stitch the incoming SR label (whose SID came from the SRMS) to the outgoing LDP label. This direction does not propagate the status of an LDP FEC signaled in ordered mode; the label binding is equivalent to the independent LDP control mode.

At least one SRMS MUST exist in a routing domain to advertise Prefix-SIDs on behalf of non-SR nodes. Several can exist for redundancy.
sections.eli5: Where the two bus systems meet, a helper swaps the old ticket for a new ticket so you can keep riding without getting off.

sections.title: The Mapping Server in Detail
sections.content:
The SRMS is a control-plane-only function that can sit anywhere in the IGP flooding scope. It uses dedicated IGP extensions for IS-IS, OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 defined in RFC 8667, RFC 8665 and RFC 8666. It consists of a Mapping Server (MS), which advertises mappings, and a Mapping Client (MC), which uses them. A node can be both. In the example, P5 advertises the mappings (P7, 107), (P8, 108), (PE3, 103) and (PE4, 104). The mappings come from local operator policy.

If an MC has both a Prefix-SID in a normal prefix reachability advertisement and a mapping server advertisement for the same prefix, it MUST prefer the reachability advertisement and ignore the mapping server one.

With several SRMSes, a node MAY advertise a preference, an unsigned 8-bit integer. The value 0 is reserved and means advertisements from that node MUST NOT be used; 1 to 255 are preferences with 255 most preferred; a node that advertises none is assigned 128. For prefixes with no Prefix-SID advertisement, the highest-preference SRMS mappings apply. Label collisions are resolved as in RFC 8660.

An SR-mapping advertisement says nothing about Penultimate Hop Popping, so other IGP-specific mechanisms MAY be used for that.
sections.eli5: A mapping server is like a school secretary who writes new bus numbers for routes the old buses cover, so new-bus drivers know about them. If a route already has its own number, the secretary's note is ignored.

sections.title: Use Cases for Partial SR Deployment
sections.content:
SR can be deployed only where its benefits are wanted. The main example keeps all traffic on LDP in steady state but uses SR to build fast reroute (FRR) backup paths. The operator wants 50 msec link-based FRR for an important service.

Without SR, protecting link BA needs a Remote Loop-Free Alternate (RFC 7490) repair tunnel to router D, which means a targeted LDP session. With SR, the repair tunnel is a node segment to D, so targeted LDP sessions are eliminated. When link BA fails, B sends the packet with the label stack {104, 202}, and after IGP convergence traffic returns to the LDP path.

For link BE there is no RLFA solution because the extended P-space and Q-space do not intersect. SR gives guaranteed FRR coverage with a repair path using node segment 106 and adjacency segment 9001 to reach G, so B uses the stack {106, 9001, 203}. The repair needs no signaling to set it up.

The RFC also sketches Inter-AS Option C (RFC 4364), where SR in one AS provides the tunnel to the border router and the packet carries three labels: the node segment, the labeled BGP route label and the service label.
sections.eli5: Normally everyone takes the old road. If the road is closed, the new system already has a detour map ready, so nobody waits for new directions.

sections.title: Manageability Considerations
sections.content:
When SR and LDP both offer an IP-to-MPLS entry for the same prefix, the LDP route SHOULD be selected by default. The reason given is that SR is expected to be introduced into networks that contain routers without SR support, so preferring LDP makes disruption unlikely. A local policy on a router MUST allow preferring the SR entry, and this policy MAY be defined locally; all routers need not use the same one.

For LSPs built by stitching LDP and SR segments, connectivity and path validation mechanisms are described in RFC 8287. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: By default everyone keeps using the old route, which is known to work. An operator can switch a router to the new route when ready.

sections.title: Migrating from LDP to SR
sections.content:
Appendix A describes a migration method inspired by the commonly used way of migrating from one IGP to another. It moves in stages.

  • T0: all routers run LDP and services ride over LDP LSPs.
  • T1: all routers are upgraded to SR with SRGB [100, 300] and node segments. Services still use LDP because it is preferred by default, but SR can already help with FRR.
  • T2: the operator enables the local policy at PE1 to prefer SR. PE1's services now ride over SR.
  • T3: the preference is gradually enabled across all edge routers. All service traffic is on SR, and LDP is still operational so services could be reverted.
  • T4: LDP is unconfigured from all routers.
sections.eli5: You test the new buses on one route, then more routes, and only retire the old buses when everything runs fine.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document introduces no change to the MPLS data plane, so no additional data-plane security is required. It does introduce another form of label binding advertisement. Its security is part of that of the routing protocols carrying it, IS-IS and OSPF, which can optionally use cryptographic authentication.

Because mapping advertisements are made on behalf of another node, they are more centralized and present a different risk profile. The RFC recognizes that configuration or programming errors could produce false or conflicting bindings and compromise forwarding. It recommends strict configuration and programmability control, monitoring of advertised SIDs, preferring a SID advertised with the prefix itself over a centralized one, and logging of any error message.
sections.eli5: The secretary's notes could contain mistakes, so you check them carefully, and trust the route's own sign first if both exist.
